Additionally, Caltech participates in the QuestBridge Program, which has a separate admissions process.\n\nRestrictive Early Action\n\nRestrictive Early Action (REA) is a non-binding early admissions process for students who are confident that Caltech is their first-choice university, are excited about the possibility of attending Caltech, and want to learn early if they are admitted to Caltech. At the same time, students will not be required to accept a Caltech REA offer and may compare financial aid options if they choose to apply to other institutions during the Regular Decision process. Although REA applications are due November 1, you will have until November 6 to submit all required and supplemental materials and standardized testing must be completed before November 30. Students will be notified of their admissions decision (admit, defer, or deny) by mid-December. Admitted students will then have until May 1, 2027 to decide if they will accept Caltech's offer of admission.\n\nStudents who choose to apply REA to Caltech may not apply Early Action nor Early Decision to any other institution, with the following exceptions:\n\nAn institution outside of the United States;\nAny public institution that has a non-binding admissions policy with a fall application deadline (such as the University of California system);\nAn institution's non-binding rolling admissions process;\nAny military academy;\nAny scholarships or special academic programs with an early deadline at another institution, public or private, if the early application submission is a necessary aspect for consideration, and the outcome is non-binding;\nIf you are deferred admission after applying REA to Caltech, you may apply to another institution's Early Decision II program. If you are admitted to that institution's Early Decision II program, you are required to withdraw your application of admission to Caltech.\n\nAdditionally, REA should be for students who are prepared to submit their most competitive application by November 1, including letters of recommendation, and required course work for admission. For fall 2027 applicants, Caltech does not require the ACT writing or science subscores. In fairness, Caltech will not consider a student\'s composite score and instead, Caltech will consider each individual subscore: Math, English, Reading, Science (optional), and Writing (optional).\n\nHow will standardized testing be used in the evaluation process?\n\nThe Admissions Committee uses standardized test scores as one data point during our holistic review process. This page is intended to help applicants understand what a typically successful applicant to Caltech looks like. Our approach to standardized testing is informed by faculty research and their understanding of how standardized test scores related to student academic performance at Caltech. Their research revealed the following results that will guide the approach to our standardized testing policy for fall 2027 first-year applicants:\n\nThere was a small difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored between a 780-800 SAT or a 35-36 ACT.\nThere was a larger, but still relatively small, difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored between a 750-770 SAT or a 33-34 ACT.\nThere was a sizable difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored a <750 math SAT or <33 math ACT or a <700 reading & writing SAT or <33 on the English exam of the ACT.\nStandardized Examination Bucket A Bucket B Bucket C\nSAT (Math or Reading & Writing) 780 - 800 750 - 770 Below 750\nACT (Individual subscore) 35 - 36 33 - 34 Below 33\nHow it appears to Admissions Shown as "Bucket A" - your exact score is hidden Shown as "Bucket B" - your exact score is hidden Your individual score is shown to the admissions committee\nWhat this means in the review process\n\nIn this new standardized testing policy, we will be using a "bucket system" when reviewing your scores in each section of the SAT or ACT. If your score falls in Bucket A or B, the admissions committee will not see whether you scored a 750 or 800 SAT (33 – 36 ACT), they will just know you\'re in a range. If your score falls below a 750 SAT or 33 ACT (Bucket C), the individual exam score will be shown to admissions committee.\n\nCaltech will continue to consider the context of your standardized testing scores and other aspects of your application during our holistic review process.\n\nCaltech Testing Deadlines for Fall 2027 Entry\nSee below for the last day which SAT or ACT scores must be submitted to Caltech. These deadlines include any test re-submissions.\nApplication Round Submission Due Date\nQuestBridge Before October 31, 2026\nRestrictive Early Action Before November 30, 2026\nRegular Decisions Before December 31, 2026\nAdvanced Placement (AP) and/or International Baccalaureate (IB) Examinations\n\nCaltech requires applicants to report all Advanced Placement (AP) and International Baccalaureate (IB) examinations taken, regardless of the score earned or whether the applicant intends for the results to be considered. Scores can be self-reported through the Beaver Breakroom. Only students who matriculate to Caltech are required to submit official exam scores.\n\nFrequently Asked Questions (FAQs)\nHow will my test scores be used in the admissions process?\n\nSAT and ACT scores are one factor within our holistic approach to admissions. High school grades and GPA are dependent on each school\'s unique grading policies and can often be difficult to decipher. SAT and ACT testing results are a standardized indicator of a student\'s readiness for the academic rigor of Caltech. However, we understand that students are more than numbers. We will review applicant\'s scores in the context of their background, resources, and personal situation as reported in their application.\n\nIs there a preferred test? If so, will there be a minimum score?\n\nThere is no preferred exam and there is no cut-off score. We accept both the SAT (paper and digital versions) and ACT tests for the standardized testing requirements, and neither is preferred over the other.\n\nVery intentionally, Caltech faculty did not decide to require a minimum score for the SAT or ACT. The test score is one data point in our review process. Read more about What We Look For.\n\nDo I need a perfect exam score to get into Caltech?\n\nAbsolutely not. Often, students will ask us if they should continue re-taking the exams to earn a perfect score. That is not a good use of your time. Traditionally, successful applicants to Caltech have had a 700 or higher on each section of the SAT or a 30 or higher on each section of the ACT. HOWEVER, there are many reasons a student may not have that score. As such, we do not have a minimum test score requirement, nor do we expect a perfect examination score.\n\nIf your score is not as strong as you\'d like it to be, you can check out the Demonstrating STEM Preparedness page to find ways to showcase additional readiness for Caltech\'s rigorous core curriculum.\n\nWill Caltech superscore the exam if I take a test more than once?\n\nYes, Caltech will superscore your tests. If you take the test multiple times, we will consider the highest score achieved in each section across all reported test dates. When a student applies, they will be asked to submit all of their test scores, at which point Caltech will create a superscore to review the applicant. We look for students who are ready not only to do the work, but to thrive in it—students who will engage difficult ideas, elevate the people learning alongside them, and keep returning to scientific questions because they genuinely want to understand, build, solve, and discover.\n\nThree Qualities, Many Paths\n\nThere is no single model of a successful Caltech applicant. Students come to science and engineering through different schools, communities, experiences, and opportunities, and they demonstrate their potential in different ways.\n\nAcross those varied paths, we look for three central qualities:\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor\nReadiness to thrive in the pace, depth, and intensity of Caltech's academic environment.\nScholarly Character\nIntegrity, resilience, and generosity in the pursuit of learning.\nScientific Drive\nRelentless and purposeful pursuit of questions, problems, and discovery.\n\nThese qualities are not a checklist, and we do not expect every student to demonstrate them in the same way. Different students bring different combinations of experiences, accomplishments, perspectives, and forms of promise. We consider your entire application and the opportunities available to you.\n\nAn image of Caltech's three qualities in what we look for in our students.\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor\nCan you thrive in Caltech's academic environment?\nReadiness to thrive in the pace, depth, and intensity of Caltech's academic environment.\n\nCaltech's curriculum requires students to engage with advanced mathematics and science from the beginning. The work moves quickly, builds rapidly, and demands more than the ability to complete difficult courses or earn strong grades.\n\nWe look for students with the academic and intellectual capacity to absorb large amounts of complex material, understand underlying ideas, and continue learning effectively as the work becomes faster, deeper, and more demanding. We consider that preparation in context, looking not only at which courses were available, but at how students engaged with the most challenging material they could access.\n\nEvidence of this capacity includes:\n\nA strong foundation in mathematics and science, including demonstrated mastery of calculus, chemistry, and physics\nDeep understanding of complex material\nThe ability to manage a demanding academic load\nSustained engagement as work becomes more difficult\n\nSimply taking advanced coursework is not the same as demonstrating a deep understanding of the material. Limited access to opportunities does not equate to limited capacity.\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor is not about surviving the Caltech curriculum. It is about demonstrating the readiness to grow, contribute, and thrive within it.\n\nScholarly Character\nWho are you when learning becomes difficult?\nIntegrity, resilience, and generosity in the pursuit of learning\n\nAcademic ability matters at Caltech, but so does the way students approach learning, challenge, integrity, and community.\n\nWe look for students who remain intellectually engaged when answers are not obvious, who respond constructively to difficulty or ambiguity, and who approach their work with honesty, humility, independence, and persistence.\n\nScholarly Character may be reflected in how a student:\n\nApproaches academic work and relationships with integrity\nRemains engaged through setbacks or uncertainty\nWorks independently and resourcefully\nRecognizes when and how to seek help\nCollaborates constructively with others\nShares ideas, questions, feedback, and knowledge generously\nMakes the learning environment stronger for the people around them\n\nCaltech students do not learn in isolation. They work together in classrooms, laboratories, residences, and research groups. We therefore look for students who will contribute not only through their individual achievement, but also through the intellectual energy, respect, creativity, and generosity they bring to the community.\n\nHigh achievement alone does not tell us how a student will respond when the work becomes difficult or how they will affect the people learning alongside them. Scholarly Character helps us understand both how a student will engage with challenges and how they contribute to the learning of others.\n\nScientific Drive\nWhat do you choose to pursue, and why?\nRelentless and purposeful pursuit of questions, problems, and discovery\n\nWe look for students who are drawn repeatedly toward questions, problems, and ideas because they genuinely want to know how and why things work. At the same time, students will not be required to accept a Caltech REA offer and may compare financial aid options if they choose to apply to other institutions during the Regular Decision process. Although REA applications are due November 1, you will have until November 6 to submit all required and supplemental materials and standardized testing must be completed before November 30. Students will be notified of their admissions decision (admit, defer, or deny) by mid-December. Admitted students will then have until May 1, 2027 to decide if they will accept Caltech's offer of admission.\n\nStudents who choose to apply REA to Caltech may not apply Early Action nor Early Decision to any other institution, with the following exceptions:\n\nAn institution outside of the United States;\nAny public institution that has a non-binding admissions policy with a fall application deadline (such as the University of California system);\nAn institution's non-binding rolling admissions process;\nAny military academy;\nAny scholarships or special academic programs with an early deadline at another institution, public or private, if the early application submission is a necessary aspect for consideration, and the outcome is non-binding;\nIf you are deferred admission after applying REA to Caltech, you may apply to another institution's Early Decision II program. If you are admitted to that institution's Early Decision II program, you are required to withdraw your application of admission to Caltech.\n\nAdditionally, REA should be for students who are prepared to submit their most competitive application by November 1, including letters of recommendation, and required course work for admission. For fall 2027 applicants, Caltech does not require the ACT writing or science subscores. In fairness, Caltech will not consider a student\'s composite score and instead, Caltech will consider each individual subscore: Math, English, Reading, Science (optional), and Writing (optional).\n\nHow will standardized testing be used in the evaluation process?\n\nThe Admissions Committee uses standardized test scores as one data point during our holistic review process. This page is intended to help applicants understand what a typically successful applicant to Caltech looks like. Our approach to standardized testing is informed by faculty research and their understanding of how standardized test scores related to student academic performance at Caltech. Their research revealed the following results that will guide the approach to our standardized testing policy for fall 2027 first-year applicants:\n\nThere was a small difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored between a 780-800 SAT or a 35-36 ACT.\nThere was a larger, but still relatively small, difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored between a 750-770 SAT or a 33-34 ACT.\nThere was a sizable difference in a student\'s grades at Caltech when they scored a <750 math SAT or <33 math ACT or a <700 reading & writing SAT or <33 on the English exam of the ACT.\nStandardized Examination Bucket A Bucket B Bucket C\nSAT (Math or Reading & Writing) 780 - 800 750 - 770 Below 750\nACT (Individual subscore) 35 - 36 33 - 34 Below 33\nHow it appears to Admissions Shown as "Bucket A" - your exact score is hidden Shown as "Bucket B" - your exact score is hidden Your individual score is shown to the admissions committee\nWhat this means in the review process\n\nIn this new standardized testing policy, we will be using a "bucket system" when reviewing your scores in each section of the SAT or ACT. If your score falls in Bucket A or B, the admissions committee will not see whether you scored a 750 or 800 SAT (33 – 36 ACT), they will just know you\'re in a range. If your score falls below a 750 SAT or 33 ACT (Bucket C), the individual exam score will be shown to admissions committee.\n\nCaltech will continue to consider the context of your standardized testing scores and other aspects of your application during our holistic review process.\n\nCaltech Testing Deadlines for Fall 2027 Entry\nSee below for the last day which SAT or ACT scores must be submitted to Caltech. Scores can be self-reported through the Beaver Breakroom. Only students who matriculate to Caltech are required to submit official exam scores.\n\nFrequently Asked Questions (FAQs)\nHow will my test scores be used in the admissions process?\n\nSAT and ACT scores are one factor within our holistic approach to admissions. High school grades and GPA are dependent on each school\'s unique grading policies and can often be difficult to decipher. SAT and ACT testing results are a standardized indicator of a student\'s readiness for the academic rigor of Caltech. However, we understand that students are more than numbers. We will review applicant\'s scores in the context of their background, resources, and personal situation as reported in their application.\n\nIs there a preferred test? We accept both the SAT (paper and digital versions) and ACT tests for the standardized testing requirements, and neither is preferred over the other.\n\nVery intentionally, Caltech faculty did not decide to require a minimum score for the SAT or ACT. The test score is one data point in our review process. Read more about What We Look For.\n\nDo I need a perfect exam score to get into Caltech?\n\nAbsolutely not. Often, students will ask us if they should continue re-taking the exams to earn a perfect score. That is not a good use of your time. Traditionally, successful applicants to Caltech have had a 700 or higher on each section of the SAT or a 30 or higher on each section of the ACT. HOWEVER, there are many reasons a student may not have that score. As such, we do not have a minimum test score requirement, nor do we expect a perfect examination score.\n\nIf your score is not as strong as you\'d like it to be, you can check out the Demonstrating STEM Preparedness page to find ways to showcase additional readiness for Caltech\'s rigorous core curriculum.\n\nWill Caltech superscore the exam if I take a test more than once?\n\nYes, Caltech will superscore your tests. We look for students who are ready not only to do the work, but to thrive in it—students who will engage difficult ideas, elevate the people learning alongside them, and keep returning to scientific questions because they genuinely want to understand, build, solve, and discover.\n\nThree Qualities, Many Paths\n\nThere is no single model of a successful Caltech applicant. Students come to science and engineering through different schools, communities, experiences, and opportunities, and they demonstrate their potential in different ways.\n\nAcross those varied paths, we look for three central qualities:\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor\nReadiness to thrive in the pace, depth, and intensity of Caltech's academic environment.\nScholarly Character\nIntegrity, resilience, and generosity in the pursuit of learning.\nScientific Drive\nRelentless and purposeful pursuit of questions, problems, and discovery.\n\nThese qualities are not a checklist, and we do not expect every student to demonstrate them in the same way. Different students bring different combinations of experiences, accomplishments, perspectives, and forms of promise. We consider your entire application and the opportunities available to you.\n\nAn image of Caltech's three qualities in what we look for in our students.\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor\nCan you thrive in Caltech's academic environment?\nReadiness to thrive in the pace, depth, and intensity of Caltech's academic environment.\n\nCaltech's curriculum requires students to engage with advanced mathematics and science from the beginning. The work moves quickly, builds rapidly, and demands more than the ability to complete difficult courses or earn strong grades.\n\nWe look for students with the academic and intellectual capacity to absorb large amounts of complex material, understand underlying ideas, and continue learning effectively as the work becomes faster, deeper, and more demanding. We consider that preparation in context, looking not only at which courses were available, but at how students engaged with the most challenging material they could access.\n\nEvidence of this capacity includes:\n\nA strong foundation in mathematics and science, including demonstrated mastery of calculus, chemistry, and physics\nDeep understanding of complex material\nThe ability to manage a demanding academic load\nSustained engagement as work becomes more difficult\n\nSimply taking advanced coursework is not the same as demonstrating a deep understanding of the material. Limited access to opportunities does not equate to limited capacity.\n\nCapacity for Caltech Rigor is not about surviving the Caltech curriculum. It is about demonstrating the readiness to grow, contribute, and thrive within it.\n\nScholarly Character\nWho are you when learning becomes difficult?\nIntegrity, resilience, and generosity in the pursuit of learning\n\nAcademic ability matters at Caltech, but so does the way students approach learning, challenge, integrity, and community.\n\nWe look for students who remain intellectually engaged when answers are not obvious, who respond constructively to difficulty or ambiguity, and who approach their work with honesty, humility, independence, and persistence.\n\nScholarly Character may be reflected in how a student:\n\nApproaches academic work and relationships with integrity\nRemains engaged through setbacks or uncertainty\nWorks independently and resourcefully\nRecognizes when and how to seek help\nCollaborates constructively with others\nShares ideas, questions, feedback, and knowledge generously\nMakes the learning environment stronger for the people around them\n\nCaltech students do not learn in isolation. They work together in classrooms, laboratories, residences, and research groups. We therefore look for students who will contribute not only through their individual achievement, but also through the intellectual energy, respect, creativity, and generosity they bring to the community.\n\nHigh achievement alone does not tell us how a student will respond when the work becomes difficult or how they will affect the people learning alongside them. Scholarly Character helps us understand both how a student will engage with challenges and how they contribute to the learning of others.\n\nScientific Drive\nWhat do you choose to pursue, and why?\nRelentless and purposeful pursuit of questions, problems, and discovery\n\nWe look for students who are drawn repeatedly toward questions, problems, and ideas because they genuinely want to know how and why things work. Students should challenge themselves by taking courses deemed appropriate by their teachers and counselors. But some students believe that “more is always better” when it comes to AP, IB or other advanced courses.\n\nWhile some students prosper academically and personally by taking large numbers of such courses, others benefit from a more balanced approach that allows them additional time for extracurricular and personal development. Even the best students can be negatively affected by taking too many courses at once, and might benefit instead from writing, reading or research projects on subjects of great interest to them.\n\nTo learn more, read our Guide to Preparing for College. To avoid the “burnout” often seen among secondary school students, please refer to our article, Time Out or Burn Out for the Next Generation.\n\nIs there a specific math requirement?\n\nApplicants to Harvard should excel in a challenging high school math sequence corresponding to their educational interests and aspirations. We recommend that applicants take four years of math courses in high school. Ideally, these math courses will focus on conceptual understanding, promote higher-order thinking, and encourage students to use mathematical reasoning to critically examine the world. Examples include rigorous and relevant courses in computer science, statistics and its subfields, mathematical modeling, calculus, and other advanced math subjects.\n\nStudents’ math records are viewed holistically, and no specific course is required. Specifically, calculus is not a requirement for admission to Harvard. We understand that applicants do not have the same opportunities and course offerings in their high schools. Moreover, many programs of study at Harvard do not require knowledge of calculus. We encourage applicants to take the courses that are available to them and aligned with their interests and goals.\n\nStudents intending to study engineering, computer science, physics, mathematics, statistics or other fields where calculus is needed may benefit from taking calculus in high school. However, students at Harvard can still pursue such fields by starting with one of our introductory calculus classes that has no high school calculus prerequisite. However, admission officers understand that not all students attend well-resourced schools throughout their lives, and that those who come from modest economic backgrounds or first-generation college families may have had fewer opportunities to prepare for standardized tests.\n\nHigh school grades in a rigorous academic program can also be helpful in assessing readiness for college courses, but the thousands of secondary schools around the country and the world employ various high school curricula and a wide range of grading systems - and some have no grades at all. Other students have been homeschooled or prepared for college by taking part in multiple schooling opportunities both in person and electronic.\n\nGiven the wide variation in how students prepare for Harvard – as well as the fact that most applicants and admitted students have outstanding academic records – it is difficult for high school grades to differentiate individual applications. That does not mean that high school grades are unimportant. Students who come to Harvard have done well day to day in their high school studies, providing a crucial foundation for academic success in college, including a 97% - 98% graduation rate.\n\nEach application to Harvard is read with great care, keeping in mind that talent is everywhere, but opportunity and access are not.\n\nWhat if it would be a financial hardship to register for the test?\n\nIf the cost of taking the SAT or ACT is of concern, keep in mind that both the College Board and ACT provide fee waivers to some domestic students from low-income families. Restrictive Early Action is a non-binding early program, signifying that if admitted, you are not obligated to attend, and have until May 1 to reply to our offer of admission.\n\nIMPORTANT:\n\nIf you are applying to Harvard under Restrictive Early Action, you may not apply to any other private institution under an Early Decision, Early Action, or Restrictive Early Action plan, or to a binding early program at a public university.\nYou are welcome to apply early to any public university, military academy, or university outside of the United States under a non-binding program.\nAdditionally, you are able to apply to other universities under their Regular Decision or Early Decision II programs.\nIf your application is deferred in the early action round, you may apply to a binding early decision program at another college (i.e. Early Decision II).\nYou may apply for scholarships or special academic programs with an early deadline at another institution, public or private, if the timing is proven to be a necessary aspect for consideration, and the outcome is non-binding.\nHarvard will meet the full financial need of admitted students regardless of whether they apply Restrictive Early Action or Regular Decision.\nIs it easier to be accepted if I apply Restrictive Early Action?\n\nHarvard does not offer an advantage to students who apply early. While admit rates tend to be higher in Restrictive Early Action, this reflects the remarkable strength of the applicant pool rather than a benefit of application timing. For any individual student, the final decision likely would be comparable whether the student applies Restrictive Early Action or Regular Decision.\n\nWhat are the benefits of applying Regular Decision?\n\nRegular Decision offers important practical advantages.\n\nYou will have more time to edit and proofread your portions of the application, and more time for your teachers and counselors to become familiar with you before they write on your behalf.\nYour application may be strengthened by senior year extracurricular achievements, course selections, academic performance, or other important factors.\nPrintable Application Forms\n\nApplications that are received in the mail will be treated equally by the Admissions Committee. More than 1,600 soldiers were housed in Harvard buildings.\n\n1861\n\nHarvard undergraduates joined the 20th Massachusetts Volunteer Regiment, nicknamed “the Harvard regiment.” On campus, Harvard students rushed to protect the cannons and ammunition held at the Cambridge Arsenal.\n\n1941\n\nDuring World War II, the U.S. Naval Reserve operated a Supply Corps School at Harvard for the training of officers, including members of the Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES).\n\nShannon Jackson\n\nAfter a career in the U.S. Navy, Shannon came to the Harvard Kennedy School as part of the inaugural cohort of American Service Fellows.\n\nRead more about Shannon\nRead more about Shannon\nDaniel Evrard\n\nDaniel, an Air Force veteran and GSAS Ph.D. student, examines decarbonization, social ties, and policy in California’s oil country.\n\nRead more about Daniel\nRead more about Daniel\nDuring my three years in the Air Force, I counseled many young service members. Parent and student loans are also available for interested families.\n\nBecause Harvard is committed to affordability, our scholarships are designed to cover 100% of your demonstrated financial need. Here is our process:\n\nFirst we determine your award by establishing your parent contribution\nThen we factor in student employment and any outside awards you’ve received\nYour remaining need will be covered by scholarship funds which are grant-based and never need to be repaid\n\nScholarship funds come from a variety of sources, including Harvard endowment funds, gifts from alumni, general tuition revenues, and federal and state grants.\n\nThe Faculty of Arts and Sciences Scholarship program includes more than 2,000 individual endowment and gift funds, established by generous alumni and donors, including a transformational $150 million gift from Ken Griffin ‘89. We report to many of these donors annually using the information students share with us over the summer.\n\nFederal and state grants\n\nIf you are a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, you may be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant or a Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (SEOG). Your eligibility is determined by the information you provide in your Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA).\n\nPell Grants and SEOG are awarded by the federal government and administered by our office, based on financial need. Within 10 days of filing your FAFSA, you will receive a Student Aid Report indicating your eligibility for a Pell Grant.\n\nIf you are a Massachusetts resident, you may also be eligible for a state Gilbert Grant, which is awarded on the basis of need. These awards do not affect your term-time work expectation.\n\nView our guide on how to complete the FAFSA\nOutside Awards\nScholarships and Grants from Outside Harvard\n\nLike many of our students, you may receive scholarship funds from sources outside Harvard, such as secondary schools, civic organizations, your parental employers, corporations, the National Merit Scholarship Programs, and the ROTC.\n\nSince the intent of these awards is that they be used for educational purposes, you must report them to Harvard and apply them toward your college expenses. Most of the information here applies to both first-year and transfer applicants, and requirements are the same for domestic and international applicants.\n\nDon\'t forget to reference our Application Tips for guidance on filling out the Common Application.\n\nApplication\n\nWe accept the Common Application. Complete and submit your materials as soon as possible to ensure full and timely consideration of your application. Your portions of the application are due by the application deadlines (November 1 for Restrictive Early Action and January 1 for Regular Decision); high school counselors are given an additional week to submit materials on your behalf.\n\nWhen you use the Common Application, you must submit your application before your supporting materials (Secondary School Report, Teacher Recommendations, etc.) can be released to a college. Do I still need to submit the midyear report?\n\nIf you study the IB curriculum or the A-level curriculum, then we expect that your school will send predicted grades, based on your current classroom work and the results of any internal or mock exams you have taken up to that point. If your school does not issue official or predicted midyear grades for your final year of school, then you do not need to submit the midyear report form, although the item may remain on your checklist.\n\nWhat if I have already graduated from high school?\n\nIf you have already graduated from high school, you should ignore the midyear report requirement (though the item may remain on your Checklist in the Applicant Portal) and simply ask your school to send a final school report if you have not already done so.\n\nTeacher Evaluations\n\nAsk two teachers in different academic subjects who know you well to complete the Teacher Recommendation forms (which includes an evaluation form and a letter of recommendation). If you wish to submit additional letters of recommendation, you can do so after you submit your application. In your application confirmation email, there will be a personalized link to send to your recommenders.\n\nWhat courses should I take to prepare for applying to Harvard?\n\nThere is no “one size fits all” rule about which curriculum to study during secondary school years. Students should challenge themselves by taking courses deemed appropriate by their teachers and counselors. But some students believe that “more is always better” when it comes to AP, IB or other advanced courses.\n\nWhile some students prosper academically and personally by taking large numbers of such courses, others benefit from a more balanced approach that allows them additional time for extracurricular and personal development. Even the best students can be negatively affected by taking too many courses at once, and might benefit instead from writing, reading or research projects on subjects of great interest to them.\n\nTo learn more, read our Guide to Preparing for College. To avoid the “burnout” often seen among secondary school students, please refer to our article, Time Out or Burn Out for the Next Generation.\n\nIs there a specific math requirement?\n\nApplicants to Harvard should excel in a challenging high school math sequence corresponding to their educational interests and aspirations. We recommend that applicants take four years of math courses in high school. Ideally, these math courses will focus on conceptual understanding, promote higher-order thinking, and encourage students to use mathematical reasoning to critically examine the world. Examples include rigorous and relevant courses in computer science, statistics and its subfields, mathematical modeling, calculus, and other advanced math subjects.\n\nStudents’ math records are viewed holistically, and no specific course is required. Specifically, calculus is not a requirement for admission to Harvard. We understand that applicants do not have the same opportunities and course offerings in their high schools. Moreover, many programs of study at Harvard do not require knowledge of calculus. We encourage applicants to take the courses that are available to them and aligned with their interests and goals.\n\nStudents intending to study engineering, computer science, physics, mathematics, statistics or other fields where calculus is needed may benefit from taking calculus in high school. However, students at Harvard can still pursue such fields by starting with one of our introductory calculus classes that has no high school calculus prerequisite. On balance, we encourage all students to master foundational mathematical material instead of rushing through any of the more advanced courses.\n\nFinal School Report and Transcripts\n\nAll admitted students who choose to enroll are required to send a Final School Report and transcript as soon as their final grades become available – no later than July 1. In exceptional cases when those tests are not accessible, one of the following can meet the requirement:\n\nAP exam results\nIB Actual or Predicted Scores\nGCSE/A-Level Actual or Predicted Results\nNational Leaving Exams Results (externally assessed) or Predictions\n\nExceptional cases typically involve a student facing challenges in paying for or accessing a test site or a student being unable to secure an available seat at a test site prior to the Regular Decision deadline. The Admissions Committee does not expect applicants to go to extraordinary measures to access SAT or ACT test sites. Applicants will have an opportunity to provide an explanation for why they are unable to submit the SAT or ACT.\n\nStudents who have other forms of testing listed above (AP, IB, GCSE, or National Leaving Exams) are still expected to take an SAT or ACT and submit those scores, if financial considerations or test availability would not limit their ability to do so.\n\nStandardized Testing FAQs\nCan I self-report my test scores?\n\nYes. Applicants may provide self-reported SAT and ACT test scores (including Subject Tests, Advanced Placement, IB, etc.). Admitted students who decide to enroll at Harvard College will be required to submit official test scores.\n\nHow do I send my official test scores?\n\nYou are free to use the College Board Score Choice option or the similar option offered by the ACT. Our official codes are 3434 for the College Board SAT Reasoning Tests and 1840 for the ACT.\n\nHow to send your SAT scores\nHow to send your ACT scores\nAre there test score "cutoffs"?\n\nThere are no score cutoffs, and we do not admit “by the numbers.” For the ACT, we will evaluate your highest composite score and any other scores you choose to share with us. We take into account your educational background when reviewing your scores.\n\nWhen do I need to take standardized tests?\n\nIf you are applying Restrictive Early Action, we would like your testing results by the end of October; however, you may submit the November series if needed.\n\nFor Regular Decision, although it is possible to submit scores from tests taken as late as the February, we recommend that you submit testing as early as possible.\n\nHow should I prepare for standardized tests?\n\nOur admissions committee understands that opportunities to prepare for standardized tests vary greatly for students of different socioeconomic backgrounds. You may find it helpful to utilize free-test prep from Khan Academy or join a free SAT bootcamp on Schoolhouse.world. The ACT provides sample tests to practice. Such free programs could help students from under-resourced schools by providing the academic tools that will serve them well on standardized tests and also in college. Students can also do well by studying widely and deeply on their own with the help of family, school, or community organizations.\n\nWhat do standardized tests and grades indicate about academic preparation for college?\n\nSAT and ACT tests are better predictors of Harvard grades than high school grades. However, admission officers understand that not all students attend well-resourced schools throughout their lives, and that those who come from modest economic backgrounds or first-generation college families may have had fewer opportunities to prepare for standardized tests.\n\nHigh school grades in a rigorous academic program can also be helpful in assessing readiness for college courses, but the thousands of secondary schools around the country and the world employ various high school curricula and a wide range of grading systems - and some have no grades at all. Other students have been homeschooled or prepared for college by taking part in multiple schooling opportunities both in person and electronic.\n\nGiven the wide variation in how students prepare for Harvard – as well as the fact that most applicants and admitted students have outstanding academic records – it is difficult for high school grades to differentiate individual applications. That does not mean that high school grades are unimportant. Students who come to Harvard have done well day to day in their high school studies, providing a crucial foundation for academic success in college, including a 97% - 98% graduation rate.\n\nEach application to Harvard is read with great care, keeping in mind that talent is everywhere, but opportunity and access are not.\n\nWhat if it would be a financial hardship to register for the test?\n\nIf the cost of taking the SAT or ACT is of concern, keep in mind that both the College Board and ACT provide fee waivers to some domestic students from low-income families. Students who are non-US citizens attending secondary schools outside the US are not typically eligible for SAT or ACT fee waivers. If applicants are ineligible for fee waivers, but still face financial hardship in paying for a SAT or ACT, the Admissions Committee still encourages these students to apply. We encourage students in this situation to take and submit results from other standardized tests to which they have greater access. For instance, students lacking access to the SAT or ACT may submit AP results or IB/GCSE/A-level/other national leaving exam predictions or results.\n\nHow will Harvard evaluate the new digital SAT?\n\nThe College Board\'s shift to a digital delivery of the SAT will not impact the way in which Harvard reviews test scores within applications. Please visit the College Board FAQs for more information.\n\nSupplemental Materials\n\nOur standard application materials typically give us ample information for making admission decisions. However, we recognize you may have truly exceptional talents or achievements you wish to share, and we want you to have every opportunity to best represent yourself.\n\nAt the discretion of the Admissions Committee, supplementary materials—such as music recordings, artwork, or selected samples of academic work—may be evaluated by faculty. These materials are entirely optional.\n\nMaterial Types\nHow to submit documents and articles\n\nScholarly articles, research, creative writing or other documents of which you are the primary author should be submitted in the Upload Materials section of the Applicant Portal. Restrictive Early Action is a non-binding early program, signifying that if admitted, you are not obligated to attend, and have until May 1 to reply to our offer of admission.\n\nIMPORTANT:\n\nIf you are applying to Harvard under Restrictive Early Action, you may not apply to any other private institution under an Early Decision, Early Action, or Restrictive Early Action plan, or to a binding early program at a public university.\nYou are welcome to apply early to any public university, military academy, or university outside of the United States under a non-binding program.\nAdditionally, you are able to apply to other universities under their Regular Decision or Early Decision II programs.\nIf your application is deferred in the early action round, you may apply to a binding early decision program at another college (i.e. Early Decision II).\nYou may apply for scholarships or special academic programs with an early deadline at another institution, public or private, if the timing is proven to be a necessary aspect for consideration, and the outcome is non-binding.\nHarvard will meet the full financial need of admitted students regardless of whether they apply Restrictive Early Action or Regular Decision.\nIs it easier to be accepted if I apply Restrictive Early Action?\n\nHarvard does not offer an advantage to students who apply early. While admit rates tend to be higher in Restrictive Early Action, this reflects the remarkable strength of the applicant pool rather than a benefit of application timing. interest can be paid quarterly or capitalized and added to the principal amount when repayment begins.\nInterest rate, fees, and repayment are the same as the Direct Subsidized Loan.\nHarvard Student Loans\n\nThe Harvard Loan is available to all need-based aid recipients, regardless of citizenship or federal aid eligibility.\n\nNeed-based loan with interest paid by Harvard during enrollment, grace, and deferment period.\nMaximum amount up to $3,500 for the academic year, or up to $1,750 per semester during fall and spring semesters.\nInterest rate fixed at 4.0 percent (5.0% for loans disbursed prior to 07/01/2016) with 10 years to repay.\nLoan is serviced through ECSI: https//heartland.ecsi.net, and applied for through the Student Loan Request Form.\nNo origination or insurance fees.\nRepayment begins six months after you graduate or drop below half-time enrollment.\nNo prepayment penalty, but repayment does not begin until separation from the College.\nFor students with a 4% interest rate, the monthly payment will be $10.12 per $1,000 borrowed, or a minimum of $50.\nDoes not require eligibility for federal loan programs.\nStudents must be Harvard Grant eligible during the academic year to use this loan program.\nAdditional loan information\nSee the Harvard Student Debt Management Guide\nGet answers to questions about Federal Direct Loans\nCheck the current federal record of your outstanding federal loans\nFind more information on private student loans.\nParent Loans\n\nYour family may choose to pursue loans to spread the cost of education over a number of years.
